The real gap is narrower: dna_embeddings has no row, despite being a Voyage-derived semantic representation of transcript excerpts — a derivative of the very source media the 72h purge exists to remove. When Google OAuth app verification (Issue 29, open) asks what derived representations of YouTube-origin content are retained and for how long, the answer for dna_embeddings is defensible but unwritten, so it gets improvised under review pressure. The same file already contains a careful asymmetry analysis for poster frames and waveform peaks (:101-102); embeddings deserve the same paragraph and do not have it.
findings.standard: A data-class retention register that the project's own process rule requires updating on every new data class ('Update this file any time data classes, retention policy, API scopes, or privacy posture changes', COMPLIANCE.md:4). Nine of 39 tables were added without the corresponding row.

domains.verdict_headline: The mechanism choices are at or above 2026 standard — the derived soft<hard<visibility invariant, the acks_late/prefetch=1/reject_on_worker_lost triple, the workload-class queue split, and the per-worker singleton loop are all what current Celery docs prescribe, each defended in DECISIONS with sources. Two things are missing: the seam between the async pattern and Celery's signal-based timeouts (run_until_complete abandons the coroutine on soft timeout, so no finally, no lock release, no pool return, no temp unlink), and any position at all on backpressure (one indivisible 8-encode message on a one-slot queue with no interactive lane). The idempotency work is excellent but guards persistence, not spend — the loser of the concurrent-generate race has already paid for an Opus-5 call before the deferred UNIQUE catches it.
strengths: visibility_timeout_s() (worker/celery_app.py:49-61) DERIVES the soft < hard < visibility invariant from CELERY_SOFT_TIME_LIMIT_S instead of hand-maintaining it, with the Celery Redis visibility caveat quoted and the exact failure it prevents named (double ffmpeg encode / double paid LLM call). This is the most commonly-missed Celery+Redis footgun and it is closed structurally.

acks_late=True + worker_prefetch_multiplier=1 + task_reject_on_worker_lost=True (celery_app.py:88-93) is exactly the combination current Celery docs prescribe, and the inline comment states the precondition it depends on (idempotent tasks, Issue 61) rather than assuming it.

The workload-class queue split (Issue 432, celery_app.py:64-84 + docker-compose.prod.yml) is the answer Celery's own optimizing guide gives for mixed long/short workloads, arrived at from a real production incident, with the `-n render@%h` vs `%%h` compose-interpolation trap documented inline so it cannot regress.

_rollback_then_unlock (worker/tasks.py:168-203) is a sophisticated read of Postgres semantics — rollback first so the unlock statement can run, and if that fails, session.invalidate() so the connection is discarded and Postgres frees the session-level lock at session end. Most codebases stop at `finally: unlock()`.

The DEFERRABLE uq_clips_video_rank used as a compare-and-set (clip_engine/ranking.py:394-438), with `if 'uq_clips_video_rank' not in str(exc.orig): raise` so a lost race is distinguished from a genuine integrity bug rather than both being swallowed.

Idempotency guards are placed at the top of the async body, not the sync shell (worker/tasks.py:2364, :3680, :3747), so they hold under redelivery AND direct invocation, and each carries the issue number that motivated it — plus _keyset_batches (:246-269) bounds sweep memory with keyset pagination rather than OFFSET on exactly the two unbounded result sets that needed it.
unmade_decisions: Backpressure and fairness: zero DECISIONS hits for backpressure/prefetch/priority. Needs a position on an interactive vs. batch render lane, per-creator in-flight caps, behaviour at queue depth N, and what the creator is told while waiting.

The idempotency house pattern as ONE entry plus a shared worker/idempotency.py helper, with the explicit rule that the key is acquired BEFORE the paid effect. Ten entries describe instances; none states the rule, so every new task re-derives it and the paid-call half keeps being missed.

Cancellation semantics of the shared per-worker loop. Issue 39 priced engine binding correctly and never priced teardown — needs either a cancel-and-drain wrapper in run_async or a written acceptance that abandonment leaks pool connections and advisory locks.

Per-workload-class time limits. One global CELERY_SOFT_TIME_LIMIT_S=3000 covers a 5-second notification email and an 8-encode render batch; only distill_style_prefs (:1573) sets a per-task soft_time_limit.

Whether the auto-render batch should remain ONE message. Download-once is right; one indivisible 8-encode message is what makes it non-preemptible and un-budgetable. A chord over a shared cached source, or a batch that re-enqueues itself after K clips, keeps the saving without the head-of-line block.

Celery version posture: pinned at 5.4.0 (April 2024). 5.5 shipped soft shutdown + REMAP_SIGTERM + worker_disable_prefetch; 5.6 shipped early 2026. No entry says whether the project tracks Celery minors or pins deliberately.
'The box is full' — what it means and who finds out. No disk alarm, no temp-file sweep, no CPU-saturation alarm, no queue-depth alarm, on a single droplet running ffmpeg + MediaPipe.

The DB connection budget for the deployment that actually exists. docs/DEPLOYMENT.md:84-105 documents a Cloud SQL/PgBouncer/KEDA inequality; the live VM arithmetic is (2 uvicorn + 4 worker children + 1 render child) x (20 main + 4 admin + 5 event_log) ~= 200 against a pgvector:pg16 container with no max_connections override (default 100). Latent at beta demand, but never written down — and db.py:60 still says 'Worker concurrency is --concurrency=2' when prod runs 4 + 1.

findings.title: run_until_complete abandons the coroutine on soft timeout — no finally, no lock release, no pool return, no temp unlink
findings.evidence: worker/celery_app.py:129-139 (run_async → _LOOP.run_until_complete); worker/tasks.py:168-203 (_rollback_then_unlock finally); worker/storage.py:245-251 (alocal_path delete=False + finally unlink); worker/tasks.py:2683; db.py:42-44 (_POOL_SIZE=15/_MAX_OVERFLOW=5); tests/test_celery_event_loop.py (5 tests, none cover abandonment)
findings.failure_scenario: An 8-clip auto-render batch crosses CELERY_SOFT_TIME_LIMIT_S=3000 while suspended at `await asyncio.to_thread(render_clip_file, …)` (worker/tasks.py:2654). SoftTimeLimitExceeded is raised in the main thread while the loop sits in epoll, so it propagates out of run_until_complete WITHOUT cancelling the task — unlike asyncio.run(), whose Runner.close() calls _cancel_all_tasks and throws CancelledError into the frame. Result: db.tenant_session.__aexit__ never runs (connection never returned → on the --concurrency=1 render worker, 20 such events permanently deadlock it on QueuePool timeout while `celery inspect ping` still answers, so autoheal never fires); the beat sweeps' `finally: _rollback_then_unlock` never runs, leaking a session-level advisory lock that the 2026-07-29 OFF_COURSE_BUGS:61 hardening cannot help because that fix assumes the finally executes; the GB-scale downloaded source is never unlinked, on a single droplet with no temp sweep and no disk alarm. Worse, the abandoned coroutine stays scheduled on the SHARED loop and can resume during a later task's run_until_complete, committing render_status=done for a clip already marked failed.
findings.standard: Celery 5.6 still has no native async worker, so a sync shell driving a loop remains the mainstream choice and Issue 39's per-worker loop + post-fork recreate_engine is the SQLAlchemy-blessed form — that part is right. But asyncio.run() cancels and drains pending tasks on teardown via asyncio.Runner.close()/_cancel_all_tasks; loop.run_until_complete() does not, leaving pending tasks unfinished. The standard remedy is to wrap run_until_complete in try/except BaseException → cancel the task → run_until_complete(gather(task, return_exceptions=True)) → re-raise.
findings.verifier_note: Real but narrower. `run_async` (worker/celery_app.py:129-139) uses loop.run_until_complete, which — unlike asyncio.run's Runner.close()/_cancel_all_tasks — does not cancel the task when SoftTimeLimitExceeded (billiard SIGUSR1, main thread) escapes while the coroutine is suspended at `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`. Verified empirically on this repo's .venv. The task is NOT lost, however: it stays pending on the shared per-worker loop and resumes on the next run_async call, running its remaining body and its finally to completion. So there is NO permanent connection-pool leak, NO permanently leaked advisory lock, and NO unreclaimed temp file — every cited `finally` does execute, just late. The actual defect is zombie-resume state corruption: (1) render_clip's `except SoftTimeLimitExceeded` (worker/tasks.py:963) writes render_status=failed, then the resumed coroutine writes render_uri + render_status=done for the same clip, leaving a 'failed' clip silently flipped to done via a path the task believes it aborted; (2) render_video_clips (worker/tasks.py:988) has no SoftTimeLimitExceeded branch, so it retries the whole batch while the zombie is still encoding — duplicate ffmpeg encode and duplicate R2 upload of the same clip_ids. Reachable only when a task exceeds CELERY_SOFT_TIME_LIMIT_S=3000 s (long ingest, or a large render_video_clips batch; a single render's own ffmpeg budget max(120, 4×duration) fires first). Severity: MEDIUM. The proposed remedy is still correct and cheap — wrap run_until_complete in try/except BaseException → task.cancel() → run_until_complete(gather(task, return_exceptions=True)) → re-raise — plus a regression test in tests/test_celery_event_loop.py, which today has 5 tests and no abandonment coverage.

findings.title: SoftTimeLimitExceeded handling is hand-applied to 5 of ~41 tasks; broad `except Exception` absorbs it everywhere else
findings.evidence: worker/tasks.py — SoftTimeLimitExceeded handled only at :430, :490, :860, :963, :7156; 91 `except Exception` and 15 `contextlib.suppress(Exception)` blocks in the same file; render_video_clips:985, clean_clip:1033, edit_clip:1256, generate_clips:917 unhandled; per-clip isolation handler at :2800; generate_clips retry at :925; existing-clips guard at :3747
findings.failure_scenario: When the soft signal lands inside the coroutine frame during clip 6 of an auto-render batch, _render_video_clips_async's per-clip handler (worker/tasks.py:2800, `except Exception … isolate per-clip transient errors`) catches it, sets clip 6 to RenderStatus.failed for no real reason, and continues to clip 7 — starting a second render_clip_file on the --concurrency=1 queue that exists specifically to guarantee one encode at a time (Issue 432), while the abandoned encode's ffmpeg thread is still running. Separately, generate_clips is a RefundOnFailureTask whose only handler is `except Exception: raise self.retry(exc=exc)`; a soft timeout during the 30-120s Opus-5 score_candidates round-trip therefore retries, and since nothing was persisted the `if not existing_clips` guard does not hold, so the retry pays for scoring again, up to max_retries=2.
findings.standard: Celery docs: soft_time_limit exists so the task can catch and clean up; hard limit is SIGKILL and nothing stops it; recommended gap 300s (which HARD_LIMIT_MARGIN_S=300 matches). The exception subclasses Exception, so any bare `except Exception` above the handler absorbs it — current guidance is to catch it explicitly and first in every long-running task. Making it structural (an AST meta-test, as tests/test_worker_invariants.py already does for the admin-session allowlist) is the repo-consistent fix.

findings.title: No backpressure decision exists: one indivisible 8-encode message on a one-slot queue, no interactive lane, no per-creator in-flight cap
findings.evidence: docs/DECISIONS.md — zero hits for backpressure/back-pressure/prefetch/priority across 13,018 lines; worker/celery_app.py:71-89 (RENDER_QUEUE, prefetch_multiplier=1); docker-compose.prod.yml render-worker --concurrency=1 -Q render; DECISIONS.md:2100 (one render_video_clips message per video); limiter.py:136-175 (daily caps, not in-flight); config.py:1144-1150 (/metrics self-disables without METRICS_TOKEN, so CELERY_QUEUE_DEPTH has no scrape target)
findings.failure_scenario: Ten creators upload within an hour on beta launch day. Ten render_video_clips messages land on the `render` queue; at the live-observed ~60-270s per encode (celery_app.py:66-68 records four clicks timing out together at ~266s each on the 4-core VM), ~80 serialised encodes = 1.5-6 hours. A creator who then clicks Render on one clip enqueues render_clip onto the same queue behind all of it — there is no interactive lane, no priority, no fairness, and no queue-depth admission control. User-visible outcome: an indefinitely spinning 'Rendering…' with no ETA and no queue-position feedback, and nothing to page on because the queue-depth gauge is not scraped.
findings.standard: Celery's optimizing guide: with mixed long/short workloads use separate worker nodes and route by run-time (the project did this once, correctly, and did not extend it to interactive-vs-batch). Redis transport supports queue_order_strategy: 'priority' + priority_steps with documented caveats. acks_late + prefetch_multiplier=1 is the documented back-pressure pairing but bounds only prefetch, not depth. 2026 guidance on oldest-job-age: shed load (429s), slow producers, or scale workers — none of which exists here since KEDA was descoped.

findings.title: The queue split's stated premise — 'network/LLM-bound tasks stay on the default celery queue' — is false for the biggest task on it
findings.evidence: worker/celery_app.py:69 (the premise comment); worker/tasks.py:2069 probe_duration_s, :2080 extract_audio_wav, :2143-2145 frame_dimensions + detect_video_camera_region, :2172-2173 detect_overlay_spans, :2390 extract_audio_events, :2605 compute_peaks — all asyncio.to_thread, all CPU-bound; docker-compose.prod.yml worker --concurrency=4 -Q celery + render-worker + uvicorn --workers 2 on a 4-core VM
findings.failure_scenario: Four concurrent ingests each run a MediaPipe camera-region consensus (up to nine 60-second decode windows per Issue 443) plus overlay-band detection plus librosa audio-event extraction, while the render worker runs a libx264 encode. Eight-plus CPU-hungry processes contend for 4 cores; the encode's wall clock inflates ~2-3x and trips render_clip_file's ffmpeg subprocess timeout (Issue 42 formula), so the clip is marked failed and RENDER_FAILURES_TOTAL increments — precisely the Issue-432 symptom the render queue was created to eliminate, now reproduced from the ingest side. The queue split fixed render-vs-render contention and left render-vs-ingest contention untouched because the premise said ingest was I/O-bound.
findings.standard: Celery's routing guidance is to split by run-time/resource class, not by nominal subsystem. The CPU class here is {ffmpeg encode, ffmpeg decode, MediaPipe/BlazeFace, librosa} and it currently straddles both queues. Fix is either routing the ingest CPU passes to the render queue or dropping the default queue to --concurrency=2 so the CPU class shares one lane.
findings.verifier_note: Real, with narrower scope and lower severity. The comment at worker/celery_app.py:68-70 ('Network/LLM-bound tasks stay on the default "celery" queue') is inaccurate for ingest_video, which runs ffmpeg decode (worker/tasks.py:2080), MediaPipe camera-region consensus (2144, flag ON in prod per docs/issues.md:2000), librosa audio-event extraction (2390) and peak computation (2605) — all CPU-bound — on the default queue at --concurrency=4, alongside the --concurrency=1 render worker and uvicorn --workers 2 on a 4 vCPU droplet with no cpu limits, no thread caps and no semaphore. Issue 432 fixed render-vs-render contention only and never considered the ingest side, and there is no DECISIONS entry for the split, so the gap is genuine. Corrections to the scenario: detect_overlay_spans is NOT part of the live load (OVERLAY_BAND_DETECT_ENABLED is false in config.py:493/.env.example:208 and still unflipped per docs/GO_LIVE.md:244 and DECISIONS.md:12971); an ffmpeg timeout raises RuntimeError which render_clip retries 3× with 60 s backoff, so most occurrences recover rather than sticking at failed; and the trigger is a single ingest overlapping a single render, not necessarily four. The 4× render budget cited as 'Issue 42 formula' is actually an unattributed comment at clip_engine/render.py:586-589. Accurate severity: LOW-MEDIUM. Accurate framing: incomplete mitigation + stale rationale comment, not an unjustified deviation. The suggested fixes (route the ingest CPU passes to the render queue, or drop the default worker to --concurrency=2) remain the right shape; capping ffmpeg/MediaPipe thread counts is a cheaper first step.

findings.title: No stop_grace_period anywhere: every deploy SIGKILLs in-flight renders after 10s, and a recovery sweep was built instead of the one-line fix
findings.evidence: docker-compose.yml / docker-compose.staging.yml / docker-compose.prod.yml — no stop_grace_period, no stop_signal on any service; deploy.yml runs `docker compose up -d` automatically on every merge to main; worker/schedule.py:42 sweep-stale-renders docstring ('renders orphaned by a worker SIGKILL (OOM / deploy teardown)'); worker/storage.py:245 (delete=False temp + finally unlink); requirements.txt:36 celery[redis]==5.4.0
findings.failure_scenario: A merge to main triggers docker-publish → deploy → `docker compose up -d`. Docker sends SIGTERM; Celery begins a warm shutdown and waits for the running task; Docker's default 10s grace elapses and SIGKILLs the child mid-encode. task_reject_on_worker_lost redelivers the message (correct), but the finally blocks never run, so the GB-scale downloaded source and the partial output mp4 are orphaned in the container's writable layer — on a single droplet with no disk-space alarm and no temp-file sweep anywhere in the repo. The project's response was sweep_stale_renders every 15 minutes (Issue 359), a recovery sweep for a root cause that is `stop_grace_period: 600s` in compose plus Celery 5.5's worker_soft_shutdown_timeout / REMAP_SIGTERM. Celery is pinned at 5.4.0, which predates both, but stop_grace_period works today regardless.
findings.standard: Celery 5.5 (2025) added soft shutdown (worker_soft_shutdown_timeout) — a time-limited warm shutdown before the cold shutdown — and officially documented REMAP_SIGTERM specifically for containerised environments where SIGTERM is the standard termination signal. The container-side half is an explicit stop_grace_period sized to the longest task.

findings.title: The (unnamed) idempotency house pattern guards persistence but not the paid call — the loser of the generate-clips race has already bought an Opus-5 scoring call
findings.evidence: clip_engine/ranking.py:401 (check-then-insert), :422-438 (deferred uq_clips_video_rank CAS, IntegrityError caught AFTER scoring); worker/tasks.py:3747 (`if not existing_clips: score_and_rank(...)`), :882 (unconditional generate_clips enqueue), :2364 (signals idempotency short-circuit); primitives at worker/tasks.py:117-165 (Redis render-start marker), :168-229 (_try_advisory_lock/_rollback_then_unlock); DECISIONS.md:10534 (SAVEPOINT+UNIQUE minute dedupe)
findings.failure_scenario: build_signals commits Signals + ingest_status=done and enqueues generate_clips (worker/tasks.py:882), then is SIGKILLed before ack. On redelivery _signals_async correctly short-circuits, then enqueues generate_clips a second time. Both executions read existing_clips == [] at :3747 because the first is still inside its 30-120s Opus-5 round-trip. Two score_candidates calls are billed to the creator's usage ledger; the loser's result is discarded when the DEFERRABLE uq_clips_video_rank fires at COMMIT (ranking.py:427). The row-duplication half is closed superbly; the double-spend half is not, and the widely-cited `if not existing_clips` guard is assumed to have closed both.
findings.standard: 2026 consensus: true exactly-once delivery is impossible; implement 'effectively exactly-once' by acquiring a client- or system-generated idempotency key IN THE SAME transaction as the business operation and BEFORE the effect — not by detecting the collision afterwards. For an external paid call with no session held, a Redis SET NX PX lease is the standard lease primitive; for an in-session critical section, a Postgres advisory lock. This project has both primitives already (_try_advisory_lock plus the Redis render-start marker) and applies them to beat sweeps but not to any paid LLM call site.

findings.title: Beat has no healthcheck and no autoheal on the live deployment, while the only 'beat HA' test pins a probe RedBeat can never satisfy
findings.evidence: docker-compose.prod.yml — beat is the only worker-family service with no healthcheck and no autoheal=true label (app/worker/render-worker have both); worker/tasks.py:228 BEAT_LOCK_SKIPS_TOTAL; config.py:1144-1150 (/metrics disabled in prod without METRICS_TOKEN); tests/test_beat_ha.py:63-77 (every assertion is a substring match over YAML; test_liveness_probe_checks_heartbeat_file asserts 'celerybeat-schedule' is present); deploy/charts/creatorclip/templates/beat/deployment.yaml:37-52; worker/schedule.py:58 + docs/RUNBOOKS.md:341 (ToS §III.E.4.b purge)
findings.failure_scenario: Beat's Redis connection wedges (single Redis container; AOF fsync stall or connection reset). The process stays up, so `restart: unless-stopped` never triggers; no healthcheck exists; BEAT_LOCK_SKIPS_TOTAL is emitted but /metrics is disabled in prod so nothing scrapes it. poll_clip_outcomes, run_lifecycle_scan, reconcile_stripe_ledger and purge_stale_youtube_analytics all stop silently — the last of which is a YouTube ToS compliance obligation, not just an operational one. Precedent for how long this goes unnoticed: health-check.yml's schedule died 2026-06-17 and nobody noticed for six weeks. Meanwhile tests/test_beat_ha.py is green, because it string-matches a Helm chart that has never run and PINS a `stat -c %Y /tmp/celerybeat-schedule` probe that can never succeed — RedBeat writes nothing to disk.
findings.standard: RedBeat stores schedule and lock in Redis and writes no schedule file, so file-mtime liveness probes do not work for it; documented approaches are a signal-registered heartbeat/PID file, direct Redis key/TTL inspection, or celery inspect. At single-VM scale the proportionate answer is a compose healthcheck asserting a live TTL on redbeat::lock plus the autoheal label — five lines, replacing a kubectl runbook that cannot be executed on the VM.

domains.domain: LLM layer: models, caching, cost, evals, resilience
domains.verdict_headline: This is the strongest domain in the repo — at or above 2026 standard on billing choke-point enforcement, prompt-injection defense, floor-gated caching that measures rather than assumes, and a golden lane that replays real recorded API bodies and fails on a model change. The gaps are in the guards, not the build: two hand-maintained test registries have drifted (one real defect — a client with no timeout at all — is live behind a green suite), nothing anywhere records which model actually served a response, and the one genuine quality instrument emits its signal to a page with no receiver. A circuit breaker is explicitly NOT what this needs at 100 users; a written position and an alarm receiver are.
strengths: billing.ledger.record_llm_usage as a single choke point verified by a repo-wide AST sweep (tests/test_usage_coverage.py layer 2) that discovers every messages.create/stream site and pins per-caller markers to a specific variable — the best-engineered test in the layer, and the pattern the two drifted registries should copy.

Prompt caching is not just applied but observed: static block first, DNA second, style notes deliberately placed AFTER the last breakpoint with the byte-prefix reasoning written out (clip_engine/scoring.py:409-427), and the log reads usage.cache_creation.ephemeral_1h_input_tokens to confirm the write landed in the 1h tier rather than the 5-min one.

stop_reason == 'refusal' is handled and degrades honestly at all three Opus 5 sites (scoring.py:476, video_context.py:409, clip_metadata.py:285) rather than indexing an empty content array — correct for a model with elevated safety classifiers fed creator-uploaded transcripts, and something most codebases get wrong.

max_tokens was raised at all three Opus 5 call sites specifically because Opus 5 thinks by default and max_tokens caps thinking+text together (1800->8000, 2000->8000, 2000->6000), with the reason recorded inline — the most common Opus-5 migration bug, caught everywhere.

test_golden_model_matches_configured_scoring_model (tests/test_scoring_goldens.py:113) turns a config model swap into a CI failure requiring re-recorded goldens — exactly the upgrade-validation mechanism the domain needs; it just only exists once.

dna_system_block returning None instead of a placeholder, with the honesty incident that motivated it written into the docstring and the disclaimer keyed off the same signal so the two cannot drift — a structural fix, not a patch.
unmade_decisions: Model-upgrade/deprecation policy: who owns a swap, what must be re-run (goldens re-recorded, live ordering lane re-run, cache floor re-checked), and the acceptance bar. Exists implicitly for scoring only, as a test.

Rolling-alias behavior-drift position: DECISIONS Issue 318 chose bare aliases over dated snapshots on deprecation grounds and never addressed silent re-pointing. Needs either 'we accept it, here is the detection' (record response.model) or 'we pin snapshots for the clip chain'.

Prompt-versioning policy: PROMPT_VERSION exists in exactly one module (analysis/video_context.py:62). Either every prompt carries one stamped on the artifact and the eval row, or write down why only the one with a persisted output needs it.
A numeric definition of 'the scorer is performing acceptably'. SCORING-MARGIN is printed with no threshold, no floor and no trend series.

Cache-floor ownership: a perishable per-model provider constant that has already flipped three times (2048->1024->2048->1024) is hardcoded twice. Needs the price-book treatment — a keyed table, a version stamp, a named re-verification trigger.
Degradation posture during a provider outage, explicitly including 'we are not building a circuit breaker at beta scale, and here is why' plus one RUNBOOKS line for the kill switch.

Whether routers/insights.py:764 keeps its own Anthropic client and hand-rolled token accounting — flagged in AUDIT_KNOWN_ISSUES.md section G as the one non-uniform call site, still unresolved, and one of the four modules the conformance registry misses.

GROUND-TRUTH CORRECTION: architecture-map C11 records the no-clients.py choice as having no linked decision. It exists at docs/DECISIONS.md:3940 (Issue 242, 2026-06-23, item 4) — but the rationale is descriptive rather than normative, and it is filed inside a transactional-email provider decision, which is why the ground-truth pass could not find it. It also flags that SOT.md documents a clients.py that does not exist; eight weeks later SOT.md:112 still says so.

findings.title: LLM conformance registry has drifted; a client with no timeout is live behind a green suite
findings.evidence: tests/test_llm_conformance.py:34 (_LLM_MODULES, 13 entries vs 17 real AsyncAnthropic clients); preference/style_distill.py:31; tests/test_model_config.py:15 (_TASK_MODEL_KEYS, 14 of 20 keys); tests/test_sdk_timeouts.py (3 of 17 clients); worker/tasks.py:1573
findings.failure_scenario: preference/style_distill.py:31 constructs AsyncAnthropic(api_key=...) with no timeout and no max_retries, inheriting the SDK's 600s default — exactly the property test_singleton_has_timeout_and_max_retries enforces, but the module is absent from _LLM_MODULES so the suite is green. Anthropic stalls on the style-distill call: the client waits up to 600s; the only backstop is Celery soft_time_limit=120, so it surfaces as SoftTimeLimitExceeded raised inside httpx rather than a typed APITimeoutError, is not caught by the module's except (RateLimitError, APIStatusError, APIConnectionError) handler, and holds 1 of 2 worker slots for the full 120s with no backoff classification. Also missing from the registries: analysis/video_context.py, knowledge/clip_metadata.py, routers/insights.py, and the STYLE_DISTILL/VIDEO_CONTEXT/CLIP_METADATA model keys. The correct pattern already exists in-repo: tests/test_usage_coverage.py layer 2 is a repo-wide AST sweep over messages.create/stream call sites; ~30 lines reuses it and closes the class permanently.
findings.standard: Conformance gates over a set of call sites are discovered, not enumerated — a hand-listed registry silently stops covering new code. This repo's own billing test already implements the discovery pattern.
findings.verifier_note: Real but overstated. ACCURATE VERSION: two hand-enumerated LLM registries have drifted — tests/test_llm_conformance.py:34 covers 13 of 17 module-level AsyncAnthropic clients, and tests/test_model_config.py:15 covers 14 of 17 per-task model keys (missing ANTHROPIC_MODEL_STYLE_DISTILL / _VIDEO_CONTEXT / _CLIP_METADATA). preference/style_distill.py:31 is the one non-conformant client: it inherits the SDK's 600s read timeout instead of the repo's 120s convention (max_retries is fine at the SDK default of 2). Concrete blast radius is small — its only caller, worker/tasks.py:1573 distill_style_prefs, sets soft_time_limit=120, which bounds the stall and is caught by the task's except/retry. The durable point is signal integrity, not this timeout: the conformance suite silently stops covering new modules, and it would not have caught this timeout even had style_distill been listed, because the assertion is `timeout is not None`, which the SDK default satisfies. The fix therefore has two parts, not one: (1) replace _LLM_MODULES/_TASK_MODEL_KEYS with the AST-discovery pattern already proven at tests/test_usage_coverage.py:236, which also asserts staleness; (2) tighten the timeout assertion to require an explicit non-default value (e.g. `timeout.read <= 300`) or it remains vacuous. SEVERITY: medium (was high) — vacuous-green/signal-integrity class, no live user-facing failure at <=100 users.

findings.title: response.model is read nowhere — a rolling alias can re-point with zero repo-visible signal
findings.evidence: observability.py:254 (record_llm_metric(model: str, ...)); billing/ledger.py:193 (record_llm_usage); clip_engine/scoring.py:466 (token log line); docs/DECISIONS.md:~11983 (Issue 318 bare-alias decision); tests/test_scoring_goldens.py:113
findings.failure_scenario: Every metric, ledger row and log line carries the REQUESTED alias from settings.ANTHROPIC_MODEL_*, never the resolved model the API returns. DECISIONS Issue 318 deliberately chose bare rolling aliases over dated snapshots because snapshots get deprecated — correct, but it never addressed that a rolling alias re-points by definition (claude-haiku-4-5 has snapshot claude-haiku-4-5-20251001). When Anthropic re-points claude-sonnet-4-6, the 11 Sonnet tasks change behavior overnight with no deploy; llm_tokens_total{model="claude-sonnet-4-6"} and every usage row keep the old string so a cost step-change has no attributable cause; the scoring goldens pin the alias, not the snapshot, so they stay green; and if a creator disputes a clip there is no record of which model produced it. One-line fix: pass getattr(response, "model", requested) into the metric/ledger and log it beside the existing token line.
findings.standard: 2026 practice pins model IDs in config and treats the provider's returned model as the audit record; deprecation discipline requires the ability to detect that the served model moved, not only to control what was requested.
findings.verifier_note:
The premise is contradicted by the vendor docs the finding should have checked. I fetched https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/overview (2026-08-17): 'Every Claude model ID is a pinned snapshot. Models with a date in the ID are fixed to that specific release. Starting with the Claude 4.6 generation, model IDs use a dateless format that is also a pinned snapshot, not an evergreen pointer. For models before the 4.6 generation, entries in the Claude API alias column are convenience pointers that resolve to a dated model ID.'

Every model this repo configures is either a pinned dateless snapshot or a terminal single-snapshot alias: claude-opus-5 (scoring / video_context / clip_metadata) and claude-sonnet-4-6 (the 11 Sonnet tasks) are both 4.6-generation-or-later dateless IDs, i.e. pinned snapshots that cannot re-point. Only claude-haiku-4-5 (hooks/chapters/performer/style_distill) is a pre-4.6 alias, and it resolves to the single existing snapshot claude-haiku-4-5-20251001. The headline scenario — 'when Anthropic re-points claude-sonnet-4-6, the 11 Sonnet tasks change behavior overnight with no deploy' — is not reachable. The requested alias IS the resolved model.

Two evidence citations are also factually wrong. billing/ledger.py:193 `record_llm_usage(creator_id, usage, cost_per_mtok_in, cost_per_mtok_out, *, cache_write_multiplier)` takes NO model argument, and the ledger write (`increment_usage(session, creator_id, period, tokens_in, tokens_out, cost)`) has no model column — so 'every usage row keeps the old string' describes a field that does not exist. The cost counter is labeled by price TIER derived from the rate (`_model_tier(cost_per_mtok_in)` -> 'haiku-tier'/'sonnet-tier'/'opus-tier'), not by an alias. Separately, the resolved model is not entirely absent from the repo: scripts/record_scoring_goldens.py:81 stores `response.model_dump(mode='json')` as each golden's `body`, which includes the response's own `model` field.

What survives is 'passing response.model into the metric label and log line would be a cheap belt-and-braces audit record' — true of any codebase, with no constructible failure at this scale, and it supports neither a 'gap' verdict nor 'high' severity. Note also that DECISIONS Issue 318's stated rationale ('Anthropic's routing resolves bare aliases to the latest stable version') is itself now stale for 4.6+, but that staleness makes the concern more moot, not less.

findings.title: Prompt-cache floor is a constant; the real floor is per-model and non-monotonic (512–4096)
findings.evidence: clip_engine/scoring.py:103 (_CACHE_FLOOR_CHARS = 4*1024); knowledge/util.py:37 (_CACHE_FLOOR_TOKENS = 1024); config.py:114-116 (documents Opus 5's 512 min, unused); config.py:117; tests/test_model_config.py:38 (_BARE_ALIAS_RE validates shape only)
findings.failure_scenario: Live docs (fetched 2026-08-17): Opus 5 = 512, Opus 4.8 / Sonnet 4.6 = 1024, Opus 4.7 = 2048, Opus 4.6 / Haiku 4.5 = 4096 — non-monotonic. (a) Today: score_candidates runs on claude-opus-5 (floor 512) but the gate demands 1024. _SYSTEM_STATIC is ~2690 chars (~670 tokens), so any creator whose DNA brief is under ~1416 chars lands in the 512–1023 band — above Opus 5's real floor, below the gate — gets no cache_control, and re-pays full Opus input ($5/MTok) on ~670 bytes-identical tokens on every scoring call, forever. (b) Reachable regression: every model key is env-overridable and test_model_config only validates alias SHAPE, not membership in a known-good set, so ANTHROPIC_MODEL_SCORING=claude-opus-4-6 passes all gates; the 1024 gate then fires below Opus 4.6's 4096 floor, emitting ttl:"1h" cache_control. Anthropic silently declines to cache and returns NO error, so every call pays the 2x 1-hour write premium with zero reads — verbatim the failure Issue 315 exists to prevent (scoring.py:13-17). Fix: a CACHE_FLOOR_TOKENS dict beside the price book, consumed by both gates.
findings.standard: Per Anthropic's current prompt-caching docs the minimum cacheable prefix is model-specific and non-monotonic across generations, and sub-floor requests are processed without caching with no error returned — so the floor must be keyed by the model actually in use.
findings.verifier_note: Real, but low severity, and only one of the two scenarios stands. ACCURATE VERSION: the prompt-cache floor is hardcoded model-independently in two places (clip_engine/scoring.py:103 `_CACHE_FLOOR_CHARS = 4096`, knowledge/util.py:37 `_CACHE_FLOOR_TOKENS = 1024`) while Anthropic's floor is per-model and non-monotonic (Opus 5 = 512, Sonnet 4.6 / Opus 4.8 = 1024, Opus 4.7 = 2048, Opus 4.6 / Haiku 4.5 = 4096). Scoring runs on claude-opus-5 (real floor 512) against a 1024-token gate, so it is conservative by 2x: with the measured 2954-char (~738-token) static block, a creator whose DNA brief is under ~1130 chars sits above Opus 5's real floor but below the gate and re-pays full Opus input on ~738 identical tokens every scoring call (~$0.003/call). Reachability is limited — dna/brief.py targets under 500 words and scoring.py:358 skips the LLM entirely with no brief — so this is a thin-channel edge case worth a few dollars a year at beta scale. The 'silently pays the 2x write premium' half is REFUTED: below the floor Anthropic performs no cache write, returns cache_creation_input_tokens=0, and the repo's 2.0 multiplier multiplies zero. The proposed fix (a CACHE_FLOOR_TOKENS dict keyed by model, consumed by both gates) is still the right shape but must also replace scoring.py:403's hardcoded `1024` literal and update the tests pinning _CACHE_FLOOR_CHARS == 4096 (test_llm_robustness.py:399-403). SEVERITY: low (was medium) — cost-efficiency polish, no correctness or billing impact.

findings.title: Model-swap validation covers 1 of 20 pinned keys; no n+1 candidate lane
findings.evidence: tests/test_scoring_goldens.py:113; config.py:102-145 (20 ANTHROPIC_MODEL_* keys); tests/test_llm_live_scoring.py:224,342; .github/workflows/llm-e2e-nightly.yml
findings.failure_scenario: test_golden_model_matches_configured_scoring_model is the only model-swap tripwire in the repo and guards ANTHROPIC_MODEL_SCORING alone. ANTHROPIC_MODEL_VIDEO_CONTEXT and ANTHROPIC_MODEL_CLIP_METADATA — the other two Opus 5 calls, and with scoring the three most expensive in the system — have none. When Anthropic announces claude-sonnet-4-6 retirement on a 60-day clock, the swap touches 11 config keys (titles, thumbnails, chat, intake, analysis, dna_brief, improvement, three per-clip features); none has a golden or an ordering probe, so the only way to learn whether title quality or DNA grounding regressed is to ship it to the beta and wait for a creator complaint. The building blocks exist: tests/test_llm_live_scoring.py already has best-of-3 ordering probes against the live API and llm-e2e-nightly.yml already runs them — the missing piece is parameterizing that lane over a CANDIDATE_MODEL env var so it reports the delta, not only the incumbent's pass/fail.
findings.standard: Run the eval suite continuously against the n+1 candidate alongside the pinned model so the migration delta is a known quantity weeks before a sunset window closes, rather than a discovery on day 28 of 60.

findings.title: The scoring-quality instrument exists, prints margins, and has no threshold, no trend store and no receiver
findings.evidence: .github/workflows/llm-e2e-nightly.yml:123-140 (SCORING-MARGIN → $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY only); no slack/notify step in any workflow (only the health-check.yml placeholder comment); analysis/video_context.py:62 (only PROMPT_VERSION in the repo); tests/test_scoring_goldens.py:102 (schema hash pinned, prompt text not)
findings.failure_scenario: A prompt edit to clip_engine/scoring.py _SYSTEM_STATIC that does not touch _OUTPUT_SCHEMA leaves every golden green (goldens replay a recorded body, and the sha256 pin covers the schema, not the prompt text). The setup-vs-aftermath margin degrades from comfortable to 2-of-3; the nightly still passes because there is no threshold. Three weeks later it tips to 1-of-3 and the nightly goes red at 03:00 UTC — with no notification step, this relies on GitHub's default scheduled-failure email, and this repo has already lost a scheduled workflow silently for six weeks (health-check.yml) and carries a job red on every merged PR since 2026-07-02 without action (OFF_COURSE_BUGS.md:42). Shipped clips drift toward aftermath windows for a month — the exact scenario Issue 476 was filed for. Because margins are printed and never persisted, 'is the scorer degrading' is unanswerable across runs. Fix using an in-repo pattern: append SCORING-MARGIN to a committed JSONL each night and fail below a ratcheted floor, identical to SCENARIO_FLOOR in tests/test_clip_engine.py. Separately, add a prompt-text sha256 beside the schema hash (~5 lines).
findings.standard: An output-quality SLO is the judge-score DISTRIBUTION tracked over time with an alert when the mean drops below a threshold or the failing rate exceeds a percentage — a one-shot pass/fail with no accumulator and no receiver is an observation, not an SLO.

findings.title: A circuit breaker and cross-model fallback are over-engineering at this scale — the missing artifact is a written position
findings.evidence: worker/tasks.py:518-526 (analyze_video_context max_retries=0, reason inline); worker/tasks.py Celery max_retries=2-3 @ default_retry_delay=60 across LLM tasks; flags.py (llm_generation kill switch, 30s TTL, no deploy); routers/clips.py:401,492,641 (kill switch + spend breaker on every LLM route); 16 of 17 clients set max_retries=2
findings.failure_scenario: Adding a Redis-backed breaker would put a new dependency in the failure path of the thing meant to protect it — and this repo already runs both the rate limiter and the spend guard fail-open on Redis by recorded decision (AUDIT_BRIEF.md section 5), so a Redis blip would disable rate limits, cost caps AND the breaker simultaneously. At <=100 users on one VM with concurrency=2, a one-hour Anthropic outage already costs: ~2 SDK retries then 2-3 Celery retries over ~3 minutes per job, clean failure, queue drains, owner flips llm_generation. What is actually missing is one runbook line ('Anthropic degraded >15 min -> scripts/flags.py llm_generation off; renders and triage continue') plus a DECISIONS entry recording that the breaker was considered and declined for beta scale — so the next refactor argues against a position instead of a vacuum.
findings.standard: Layered resilience (retry -> fallback chain -> circuit breaker, ~5 failures to trip / 60s cooldown) is standard at scale, but the same guidance's load-bearing caveat is that every reliability layer must itself have a fallback; a breaker whose state lives in an already-fail-open Redis is net-negative here.
findings.verifier_note:
I tried to kill this and every cited fact resolved. worker/tasks.py:518 is `@celery.task(bind=True, max_retries=0, name='worker.tasks.analyze_video_context')` with the reasoning inline in the docstring ('the SDK's built-in max_retries=2 already covers transients, and a broken context pass must never refund or re-deliver'). `grep default_retry_delay` confirms 30/60/120s across the LLM and render tasks at max_retries=2-3. routers/clips.py:403, 492 and 641 all carry `dependencies=[Depends(require_flag(...)), Depends(require_budget)]` plus stacked slowapi limits. flags.py:41 `FLAG_TTL_S = 30.0` with DB-backed resolution (not Redis), so the kill switch genuinely propagates in ~30s with no deploy and is NOT co-dependent with the fail-open Redis paths. docs/AUDIT_BRIEF.md:168 states verbatim that the rate limiter and spend guard fail open on Redis and names the compounding risk. 16 of 17 Anthropic clients set max_retries=2 explicitly (style_distill inherits the SDK default of 2, so effectively 17/17).

The 'missing artifact' claim also checks out: `grep -i 'circuit breaker' docs/DECISIONS.md` returns nothing, and docs/RUNBOOKS.md mentions Anthropic exactly once (line 436, a breach-notification row) with no degradation or kill-switch procedure. There is genuinely no written position and no runbook step.

One soft spot I could not turn into a refutation: the argument leans on 'a Redis-backed breaker adds a dependency to the failure path', but a breaker at concurrency=2 on a single VM could be purely in-process and add no dependency at all, so that particular rebuttal is a partial strawman. It does not change the conclusion, which rests on independently verified ground: the existing retry ladder plus a 30s DB-backed kill switch already bounds a provider outage to roughly 3 minutes of doomed retries per job with a clean queue drain, and there is no cross-model fallback chain to guard because models are per-task pinned in config. Severity 'low' and judgement_call=true are honestly stated, and the proposed deliverable (one runbook line plus a DECISIONS entry recording the decline) is proportionate to the scale.

domains.domain: Clip engine, ML boundary, and eval methodology
domains.verdict_headline: The deterministic geometry half of this engine is measured better than almost any solo project, and the Issue-476/480 lane genuinely moved the LLM scorer from "evaluated nowhere" to "evaluated thinly". The learning half is broken in a way no gate can see: LightGBM's untouched min_child_samples=20 makes the preference model a provably constant predictor for every label count from 20 to ~43 — exactly the band the maturity ramp covers — so personalization is a measured no-op over its entire ramp while the API reports it active. The test written four days ago to guard precisely this passes only because its fixture is the one 40-row configuration where LightGBM can split.
strengths: The geometry eval is the best-defended gate in the repo: 32 scenarios, a 100% pass-rate assertion, a ratcheted SCENARIO_FLOOR=31 (tests/test_clip_engine.py:269), a regex scan forbidding unapproved skip/xfail with an empty allowlist, and CI enforcement as a COMMIT STATUS rather than a required job — because GitHub reports a skipped required job as success (Issue 265). One invariant defended properly.

tests/test_scoring_goldens.py is current-standard: real recorded Anthropic response bodies replayed through anthropic.types.Message.model_validate into the REAL parse path, a genuine stop_reason='max_tokens' truncation golden, and a sha256 pin on _OUTPUT_SCHEMA that reds CI until a ~$0.20 re-record.

findings.title: LightGBM is a constant predictor for label counts 20–43: the entire personalization ramp is a measured no-op while the API reports active=true
findings.evidence: preference/model.py:206 (LGBMClassifier with all regularisation defaults); preference/model.py:196-208 (branch at n>=20); preference/model.py:162-167 (weight ramps 0→0.5 over n=20→40); config.py:602 (PERSONALIZATION_THRESHOLD_LABELS=20); clip_engine/ranking.py:220-228 (blend written to blended_score); routers/clips.py:786-792 (active = weight>0)
findings.failure_scenario: Creator triages 30 clips (18 kept / 12 dropped). retrain_preference → fit(n=30) → LightGBM branch. LightGBM's default min_child_samples=20 requires ≥20 rows in BOTH children, so no split is legal: the booster has 1 tree, 0 splits, and predict_proba returns an identical constant c for every clip. rerank_with_preference writes blended_score = 0.75*score + 0.25*c, strictly monotone in score, so the persisted rank order is byte-identical to DNA-only. GET /videos/{id}/clips simultaneously returns personalization {active:true, labels:30, weight:0.25} and blended_score IS NOT NULL (which the Issue-465 contract defines as 'personalization was applied'). Measured on pinned lightgbm 4.6.0 with realistic feature draws: 200/200 trials degenerate at n∈{20,25,30,35,40}; 0/200 at n>=44. verbosity=-1 suppresses LightGBM's own 'no further splits' warning. Corollary: the LogisticRegression branch (n<20) is unreachable at serve time because preference_weight returns exactly 0.0 there and rerank early-returns — so NO label count below ~44 has ever influenced a served ranking.
findings.standard: DECISIONS.md:9066 chose the maturity gate as 'the standard hybrid cold-start strategy — start content-based, grow personalization as feedback accumulates'. The recorded intent is a ramp; the implementation is a step function at n≈44 with a 24-label dead zone. Standard practice for GBDT below a few hundred rows is to explicitly shrink min_data_in_leaf/num_leaves, or not use GBDT at that volume.
findings.verifier_note: LightGBM is a constant predictor for label counts 20–40 (measured: 200/200 degenerate at n=38–39, 198/200 at n=40, 1/200 at n=41, 0/200 at n>=42). The dead zone is 21 labels wide, and the transition is at n=41, not ~44. Because preference_weight returns 0.0 at exactly n=20, the window in which the API reports personalization active while the served ranking is byte-identical to DNA-only is n=21..40 — 20 label counts. The finding's central claim is if anything strengthened by the correction: the weight ramp spans exactly n=20→40 and reaches PREFERENCE_WEIGHT_CAP at n=40, so the ENTIRE ramp lies inside the degenerate zone and the model only becomes non-constant at n=41, by which point the weight is already saturated at the cap. Everything else — mechanism (min_child_samples=20 x min_data_in_bin=3), reachability, the strictly-monotone-blend argument, the active=true/blended_score-not-NULL contradiction, the unreachable-LogisticRegression corollary, and the HIGH severity — stands as written.

findings.title: The Issue-480 rerank eval is green only because its fixture is the single knife-edge 40-row shape LightGBM can split — new vacuous-green instance on the newest gate

findings.standard: AUDIT_BRIEF.md §6 names this exact family: an intermediate layer reports success without exercising the thing it claims to verify. I tried hard to kill this as a duplicate of F1 or as verifier taste, and failed on both counts.

CITATIONS RESOLVE: tests/preference/test_rerank_eval.py:105-131 are `test_label_set_hits_lightgbm_branch_at_cap_weight` (with the `scorer.label_count == 2 * PERSONALIZATION_THRESHOLD_LABELS` assert at exactly :115) and `test_trained_model_orders_upvoted_pattern_above_downvoted`. Dumping the booster shows every tree's root split is `has_retention_spike` at threshold ~1e-35 with left_count=20 / right_count=20 — literally the only partition of 40 rows that satisfies min_child_samples=20 on both sides.   20/20 → 92 trees, spread 0.999903
  24/16 → 1 tree,  spread 0.000000
  27/13 → 1 tree,  spread 0.000000
  30/10 → 1 tree,  spread 0.000000
So the green is entirely an artifact of the 20/20 balance. NOT A DOCUMENTED CONVENTION: nothing in AUDIT_BRIEF.md §5, AUDIT_KNOWN_ISSUES.md, or DECISIONS.md acknowledges the fixture's balance as deliberate. The docstring's stated rationale for the 40 rows is only 'LightGBM branch + weight at cap'; the 20/20 split is unremarked, which supports the finding's read that it came along for free.

CONTROL CLAIM VERIFIED: `test_control_weight_zero_preserves_dna_order` exists at :162 and works by driving weight to 0 — it proves the harness can go red, but probes nothing about booster degeneracy.

SEVERITY: high holds and is not double-counting F1. findings.title: The efficacy harness has no DNA-only ablation arm, so it cannot measure the preference model's marginal contribution and cannot detect the degeneracy
findings.evidence: preference/efficacy.py:210 (RANKINGS = random, generic_signal, dna_preference); preference/efficacy.py:262 (generic_signal = clip_engine.scoring._signal_score, a different ranker); preference/efficacy.py:326-348 (_blend_scores); worker/tasks.py:1877-1898 (NDCG warn-ratchet)
findings.failure_scenario: With a degenerate scorer, _blend_scores returns a strictly monotone transform of c.dna_composite, so ndcg['dna_preference'] equals the DNA-only NDCG to full float precision. But no arm computes DNA-only NDCG, so the equality is unobservable. The per-retrain warn-ratchet only fires on a drop of >0.05 versus the PREVIOUS model version; a model contributing exactly zero lift since inception never drops and never warns. The one question the harness exists to answer — 'is personalization helping this creator?' — requires an ablation control it does not have. Fix is one dict entry: 'dna_only': [c.dna_composite for c in eval_clips].
findings.standard: Offline ranking evaluation requires the production system minus the component under test as the control arm. Otherwise you measure the whole stack against an unrelated baseline and can never attribute lift. Everything else in this harness (chronological split, graded relevance, paired bootstrap CIs, Kendall tau) is at current standard.

findings.failure_scenario: The question the Opus 5 upgrade was bought to answer — 'are the clips better?' — has a data substrate accumulating for weeks that no query, metric, dashboard or Prometheus gauge reads. findings.standard: Position bias makes raw click/keep data a sub-optimal training and evaluation signal; the standard correction is IPS (reweight by inverse probability of observation at that position), with 2026 refinements (affine / control-function) for trust and selection bias. At <=100 users an A/B test of two rankers cannot reach power; interleaving is the documented answer (10–100x more sensitive, >100x fewer users for 95% power, 82% agreement with A/B verdicts at 4% of traffic).

findings.title: 25 serialized backend fields reach no human, including two shipped transparency features and two thirds of the BFF envelope deviation

ClipOut.has_crop_track unmodelled -> hooks/useCropTrack.ts:20 fetches /clips/{id}/crop-track per clip and swallows the 404.
findings.failure_scenario: A video whose transcription fell back to Deepgram's one-utterance output sets degraded='no_utterances'; FullTranscriptPanel renders it as an ordinary transcript (one giant segment) with no indication, and the creator trims against a transcript the system already knows is bad. Separately, a video past 100 clips after repeated 'Generate more clips' passes (Issue 431, 12/pass) silently loses the tail from the review queue because truncated is never read.
findings.standard: In a co-owned BFF monorepo the deviation from strict REST is defensible (DECISIONS 5493 argues it well), but the deviation only pays if the client consumes the envelope. Current practice for one-directional drift like this is a generated contract plus a CI diff, which turns 'field added, nobody wired it' from an invisible omission into a compile error at the point of generation.
findings.verifier_note: Verdict label `deviation-unjustified` -> `partial-adoption` (or fold into closed-loop-type-contract as its measured consequence). The DECISIONS.md:5493 BFF-envelope deviation is justified and sourced, and its load-bearing element `message` IS consumed at three call sites; the defect is that `state`, `next_action`, and 25 other serialized fields were never wired client-side. Two factual corrections to the evidence: (1) `degraded` does NOT reach zero humans — worker/tasks.py:2306-2311 emits it as an SSE step (label='transcript_degraded') and useStageStream.ts:78 -> StageStepper.tsx:73 renders step labels generically with no allowlist, so it flashes as a raw snake_case string during ingest before being overwritten by 'store_transcript'; the correct claim is that no DURABLE surface reads it, so a creator who was not watching the progress stream trims against a transcript the system knows is bad. (This also exposes an unflagged issue: internal step labels are rendered to users verbatim.) (2) The `truncated` scenario requires ~9 'Generate more clips' passes on one video (_LIST_LIMIT=100, 12 clips/pass per Issue 431) — real but rare at beta scale. Severity medium is correct.

findings.title: a11y gate is pinned to WCAG 2.1 tags, so axe's target-size rule has never run against 3px timeline handles
findings.evidence: frontend/e2e/a11y.spec.ts:44 `.withTags(['wcag2a','wcag2aa','wcag21a','wcag21aa'])` -- wcag22aa absent; axe-core's target-size rule is tagged wcag22aa and is off by default. frontend/src/components/editor/Timeline.tsx:263 styles each cut edge 'absolute inset-y-0 w-[3px] cursor-ew-resize bg-danger'. a11y.spec.ts:50-52 filters to serious||critical only. grep docs/DECISIONS.md: 'WCAG 2.2' 1 incidental hit, 'target size' 0. Credit where due: Timeline.tsx:250-256 and TimelineRail.tsx:239-245 implement role=slider + tabIndex + aria-valuemin/max/now/valuetext, and TimelineRail.tsx:70-71 documents the role=group choice citing MDN.
findings.failure_scenario: Issue 134 removes filler words and 150ms silences, so a cut can be a fraction of a second wide; at default zoom its start and end handles sit a few px apart. SC 2.5.8 requires 24x24 CSS px or a 24px non-intersecting spacing circle -- a 3px handle fails the size test and adjacent handles fail the spacing exception. A creator on a touch device or with a motor impairment cannot reliably grab either edge, and no gate reports it because the rule that reports it is not enabled.
findings.standard: The 2026 bar is WCAG 2.2 AA, not 2.1. EN 301 549 v4.1.1 -- the technical standard behind European Accessibility Act compliance -- aligns to WCAG 2.2. The 2.2 criteria that bite an editor UI are 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum, 24x24 CSS px) and 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured. Add 'wcag22aa' to withTags and triage; if you conclude 2.5.8's Essential exception applies to frame-accurate timeline handles that is a legitimate answer -- but it must be written down, and currently there is no answer at all.

findings.title: Zero frontend coverage measurement; 14 of 15 hooks untested, including the edit-persistence CAS path
findings.evidence: frontend/vite.config.ts test block has no coverage key; @vitest/coverage-v8 absent from package.json devDependencies. 92 test files / 168 source files. 14 of 15 src/hooks/*.ts have no colocated test -- useEditDocument.ts (autosave + revision CAS), useUploader.ts (Uppy multipart to R2), useCropTrack.ts, useClipRender.ts, useApplyClipMetadata.ts. 11 of ~22 src/lib/*.ts untested, including keyboard.ts (the Issue-390 keyboard bus), clipPiles.ts, schedule.ts, timecode.ts.
findings.failure_scenario: useEditDocument's conflict path (server 409 on a stale revision -> refetch -> reapply) is exercised by no test. A regression there silently discards a creator's trim edits while SaveStatus reports saved -- the identical shape to OFF_COURSE_BUGS.md:22, where YourCall.tsx:124 rendered 'Error - try again' in success green and discarded the rating. Editor.test.tsx and editor-persistence.spec.ts may cover it indirectly; without measurement nobody can say which.
findings.standard: 2026 practice is coverage-as-map, not coverage-as-target (Testing Trophy). Vitest supports thresholds incl. per-file, but guidance is 'begin from measured reality, protect new code'. Recommendation for THIS repo: add @vitest/coverage-v8 with reporters and thresholds UNSET; use it once to pick 3 hooks to test; do NOT add a floor. Issue 479 already showed what a number-shaped frontend gate would become here -- per-module and diff-cover floors silently no-op'd from 2026-06-23 to 2026-08-12 while printing 'All runnable gates passed'. Making the existing 92 files block a merge (finding 2) is worth more than measuring the ones that do not exist.

findings.title: One 887 KB chunk, no code-splitting, no budget -- risk over-stated, but the decision vacuum is real
findings.evidence: frontend/dist/assets/index-DJ9gBY7A.js = 887,823 B raw / 261,004 B gzip / 215,633 B brotli (built 2026-08-15); index-Bbw2H-EN.css = 58,847 B / 11,255 B gz. dist/index.html loads ONE <script type="module">. Zero React.lazy, zero Suspense, zero manualChunks in vite.config.ts. Mitigations verified: App.tsx:66-73 documents that `/` is a server-rendered static/landing.html, so anonymous marketing traffic never loads the bundle; Waveform.tsx is DPR-aware with redraw-on-effect (no per-frame RAF). grep docs/DECISIONS.md: 'code-split' 0 hits.
findings.failure_scenario: /app/login -- the first authenticated hop -- downloads all 261 KB gz (Uppy, Radix, the full editor, the canvas timeline) to render a Google sign-in button. On a cold mobile connection that is a multi-second delay before any interactive element; at 261 KB gz the app is above the 2026 INP-linked working budget. Consequence is a slower first sign-in, not a broken feature.
findings.standard: 2026 budget for initial JS is <200 KB gz (aggressive) or <150 KB gz mobile-first, with JS payload named the single largest predictor of INP. Judgement call: at <=100 desktop creators on a repeat-visit authenticated tool behind Cloudflare with content-hashed assets, this is a 'you do not need this at 100 users' item -- do NOT start a code-splitting programme. Write one DECISIONS line (single chunk; budget 300 KB gz; revisit trigger = mobile becomes a real surface or the budget is crossed). React Router v7 Data Mode makes route-level `lazy` a 3-line-per-route change later, so deferring costs nothing.
findings.verifier_note: No correction required. One footnote for the report: frontend/dist/ is gitignored (frontend/.gitignore:11), so the byte counts come from a local 2026-08-15 build rather than a committed or prod-pulled artifact — representative, since prod builds the same source in the Dockerfile frontend-build stage, but the measurement should be re-taken from a CI/Docker build if the budget is ever written into a gate.

findings.title: React Router v7 Data Mode (router-only, zero loaders) + TanStack Query v5 as the single cache is the correct 2026 pairing
findings.evidence: frontend/src/App.tsx uses createBrowserRouter with ZERO loader and ZERO action -- Data Mode is used only for nested layout contexts and the route-level errorElement (RootError, Issue 346). One QueryClient (staleTime 30s, retry 1, refetchOnWindowFocus false, rationale in-file). One ES-module singleton store, stores/activeTasks.ts; Zustand explicitly rejected at docs/DECISIONS.md:11500 (Issue 211). grep 'react-router' docs/DECISIONS.md -> 0 hits.
findings.failure_scenario: No failure. The recorded risk in this area -- duplicating a cache between router loaders and TanStack Query, producing two sources of truth that disagree after a mutation -- cannot occur here because no loaders exist. The only exposure is that the correct choice is undocumented, so a future session could 'modernize' to TanStack Router or move fetching into loaders and reintroduce the double-cache problem with no recorded position to argue against.
findings.standard: Current guidance is explicitly not to duplicate caching between router loaders and a query cache; using React Router purely for routing/layouts/error boundaries with TanStack Query owning server state is a recommended arrangement. TanStack Router's advantages (typed routes, built-in SWR) do not justify migration when Query already owns the cache. No change recommended -- only a DECISIONS entry recording that this is deliberate.

domains.verdict_headline: The three-layer tenancy model and the erasure machinery are genuinely above standard for an 82-day-old solo project — required-argument GUC seam, test-pinned admin allowlist, and an R2 enumeration that reaches orphans a prefix sweep cannot. The failure is in the availability-and-cost control plane: the most-documented "deliberate decision" in this domain — that the rate limiter fails open — is NOT what the code does, and I reproduced the opposite empirically. Combined with a /health endpoint that returns 200 during a total outage, a Redis latency spike is a silent full user-facing outage that the only continuous uptime signal reports as green.
strengths: db.py::tenant_session(creator_id) makes the RLS GUC a REQUIRED argument, so a call site structurally cannot forget it; cross-tenant sweeps must use AdminSessionLocal and that allowlist is pinned by tests/test_worker_invariants.py:172. The type system enforces what convention cannot — the best single control in this domain.
routers/_owned.py: 47 lines, one generic get_owned(), one query, 404 for both missing and foreign, documented as defence-in-depth UNDER RLS rather than as the isolation mechanism.

Migration 0045's NULLIF hardening of the GUC converts an empty-string-on-pooled-connection crash (OFF_COURSE_BUGS.md:90 — policies 500'd instead of denying) into a deny, and writes the incident into the migration.

worker/erasure.py enumerates DB pointers UNION deterministically constructed keys, which reaches the clean-confirm orphans that have no row pointing at them; each KEY_PATTERN is pinned by tests/test_erasure_keys.py. Closes the clips/ namespace worry raised in AUDIT_KNOWN_ISSUES sec.F. All 28 creator_id FKs are ondelete=CASCADE and event_logs (the one table with no FK) is purged explicitly.

routers/auth.py:568-575 writes the deletion audit row with the creator UUID and deliberately NOT the email or channel_id, with the reasoning inline — PII in a never-purged RLS-exempt table would let erased data survive the erasure. Many mature products get this wrong.

crypto.py is 55 clean lines: MultiFernet primary+previous, lru_cache singleton with a documented cache-clear contract, TokenDecryptError carrying no ciphertext, and config.py:1059-1075 rejects a malformed TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY_PREVIOUS before it can silently break a live rotation window. Redis persistence is also correctly configured (docker-compose.prod.yml:118, AOF everysec + RDB), so spend counters survive a restart rather than silently zeroing the caps.
unmade_decisions: A single fail-open/fail-closed posture table: which Redis-dependent controls fail open, which fail closed, and why. Currently asserted in five docstrings and one DECISIONS entry, and contradicted by the code in the one case that matters. The correct asymmetry is available in two lines: Limiter(in_memory_fallback_enabled=True) gives the local token bucket (slowapi already implements the _storage_dead circuit breaker at extension.py:634-640, inert only because the flag is off), and the spend guard should then fail CLOSED because it becomes the only thing between a bug and an unbounded Anthropic bill.

'One creator = one login, no team seam in v1' as an explicit bet — the largest structural bet in the tenancy model with zero recorded position. The 27 RLS policies are the CHEAP part (one mechanical migration, the tenant_session seam does not change shape); the expensive part is that `creators` is simultaneously tenant and principal, and the JWT `sub` is used interchangeably for 'who is acting' and 'whose data'. Take the cheap half now: add a distinct `tid` claim alongside `sub` (~10 lines, a no-op today since tid == sub) so the conflation becomes explicit before the first paying cohort makes it expensive.

What /health means. It is currently liveness, readiness and dependency-status at once, and the compose healthcheck and the Cloudflare runbook read it two different ways. Split /health (liveness) from /ready (dependency-gated 503) and point the uptime monitor at /ready.

RLS coverage as a DERIVED property: a test reading information_schema.columns for creator_id and asserting a matching pg_policies row + relforcerowsecurity. This is the mechanism the project has twice identified after a Class-7 incident and twice not built.

JWT signing-key rotation — a `kid` header plus a JWT_SECRET_KEY_PREVIOUS accepted-key list, mirroring the MultiFernet pattern crypto.py already establishes. JWT_SECRET_KEY is currently the only credential whose compromise has no graceful remedy: every session for every creator becomes forgeable and the only fix is a hard swap with no runbook. This matters far more than JWT revocation, which at a <=100-user beta with no privilege-escalation path is a defensible 60-minute window.

Derived-data retention under the YouTube ToS: a written position on whether Creator DNA, dna_embeddings, video_insights and videos.title/published_at/duration_s for origin=youtube rows sit inside or outside the III.E.4 / III.D.2.3 perimeter. This is the question the compliance audit triggered by the quota-extension request will ask.

A secrets-of-record decision. Application secrets are handled well; infra secrets live only in a hand-edited /opt/autoclip/.env with no history, where a typo on TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY is unrecoverable (every stored OAuth refresh token becomes undecryptable). SOPS+age is the proportionate 2026 answer for a single self-hosted VM (encrypted file in git, no service to run, git history as versioning); Infisical if a UI is wanted; Doppler is ruled out by the stays-on-my-box preference. 'Not yet at 100 users' is a legitimate answer — but it should be written down, and the escrow half (Issue 255) is not optional.

Structural pin on the GDPR export's contents. _collect_creator_export (worker/tasks.py:5153-5230) is clean today — it does not touch youtube_tokens or creator_api_keys and Creator carries no secret columns — but _row_to_dict (:5148-5150) blindly serializes every column of whatever model it is handed, and no test asserts the absence of *_encrypted / key_hash. Same latent-trap shape as the Stripe amount_total gap already filed.

findings.title: The rate limiter fails CLOSED with an unhandled HTTP 500, not open — the decision on record is the opposite of the code
findings.evidence: limiter.py:129-133 (no swallow_errors, no in_memory_fallback); main.py:145-147; .venv slowapi 0.1.9 extension.py:631-646 re-raises; docs/DECISIONS.md:2634-2636; limiter.py:42-44,148-151; docs/AUDIT_BRIEF.md sec.5 row 1; run_layer0.py:334 (99% coverage floor on limiter.py); tests/test_rate_limiting.py (21 tests, zero for Redis-down)
findings.failure_scenario: Redis on the prod VM stalls >100ms (socket_timeout=0.1, limiter.py:83-86 — a BGSAVE fork or CPU starvation from the two concurrent ffmpeg/MediaPipe encodes is sufficient; Redis need not be down). Every decorator-limited route raises redis ConnectionError/TimeoutError which slowapi re-raises -> FastAPI 500. That includes GET /auth/me (routers/auth.py:401, 120/minute) which the SPA AuthGate calls on every load, and the OAuth callback (20/minute). Nobody can sign in and nobody signed in can use the product. Reproduced with .venv/bin/python + TestClient against a dead Redis port using limiter.py's exact construction args: status 500, endpoint body never executed.
findings.standard: 2026 consensus is asymmetric by control type: availability controls fail open via a LOCAL in-memory token bucket plus a circuit breaker (not 'skip the check'), money/authorization controls fail closed. The inverse bug (fail-closed on Redis outage) is a known 2026 defect class in the wild.
findings.verifier_note: Keep the finding and its severity, but restate the standards basis. Accurate version: 'The limiter is constructed with neither swallow_errors nor in_memory_fallback (limiter.py:129-133), so slowapi 0.1.9 re-raises any redis error (extension.py:630-645) and — with no catch-all handler in main.py — every rate-limited route returns HTTP 500 while the endpoint body never runs (reproduced against a dead Redis port with the module''s exact construction args). This directly contradicts three project documents that state the limiter fails OPEN: docs/DECISIONS.md:2633-2634, docs/AUDIT_BRIEF.md §5 row 1, and limiter.py''s own docstring at lines 42-44. It is additionally a vacuous-green-signal instance: the sole Issue-312 test (tests/test_rate_limiting.py:278) asserts only that the socket_timeout kwarg is set, never that a Redis failure degrades gracefully, under a 99% coverage floor (run_layer0.py:333). Drop the claim that fail-open is the 2026 consensus — it is not (Envoy defaults failure_mode_deny=true; the literature is explicitly context-dependent). The defensible standard is graceful degradation to a local in-memory bucket instead of a 500, and the defensible finding is decision-vs-code divergence plus an untested failure path. Fix: either set in_memory_fallback_enabled=True (matching the documented posture) or amend all three documents to state the limiter fails closed — and add a test that exercises a request with Redis unreachable.'

findings.title: /health returns 200 "degraded" when Redis is down; the runbook claims 503 — a total outage presents as green
findings.evidence: main.py:553-567; docs/DEPLOYMENT.md:162-163 ("degrades to non-ok + 503"); docker-compose.prod.yml:22-30 (healthcheck comment deliberately treats degraded as alive); process-map.md sec.6 (CF Health Check is the only continuous uptime signal; zero alert rules repo-wide)
findings.failure_scenario: Redis degrades -> every user-facing route 500s (see limiter finding) -> /health answers 200 {"status":"degraded","redis":"error"} -> the Docker healthcheck is satisfied so autoheal does not fire -> the Cloudflare Health Check sees 200 and stays green. Nothing else fires because there are zero alert rules in the repo. Same shape as the 9-day silent outage at OFF_COURSE_BUGS.md:104. The only mitigation is DEPLOYMENT.md:156 step 3's manual Cloudflare response-body match on "status":"ok" — unverifiable from the repo, and undermined six lines below by the false claim that the endpoint returns 503 anyway.
findings.standard: Split liveness (/health, 200 whenever the process serves) from readiness (/ready, 503 when a hard dependency is down) and point the external uptime monitor at the dependency-gated one. A single endpoint that is simultaneously liveness, readiness and dependency-status will be read two different ways by two different consumers — which is exactly what happened here.
findings.verifier_note: Downgrade from 'gap / high' to a documentation defect, SEV3/low. Accurate version: 'docs/DEPLOYMENT.md:162-163 states that /health "degrades to non-`ok` + 503 when a backing service is down". It does not — main.py:553-567 always returns 200, with only the JSON status flipping to "degraded". The 200-on-degraded behavior itself is deliberate and documented (docker-compose.prod.yml:23-24: liveness-only, so a dependency blip does not trigger an autoheal restart), and the runbook''s own step 3 (DEPLOYMENT.md:156) already compensates by requiring a Cloudflare response-body match on "status":"ok". The risk is that the false 503 sentence six lines below could lead an operator to configure status-code matching only and lose the sole dependency-aware alert. Fix: correct the sentence to describe the actual contract, and note that the body match is load-bearing, not optional. Do NOT file this as a missing-alerting finding — that is #282/#236 in docs/GO_LIVE.md, an explicit owner deferral for the friend beta with written re-open criteria. Do not cite the "9-day silent outage" as precedent; that framing was retracted in GO_LIVE.md:82 and PROJECT_STATE.md:269-271 (it was ~31h and an intentional owner poweroff).'

findings.title: The spend guard's Redis client has no socket timeout — a Redis stall hangs require_budget forever and 'fail open on error' never fires
findings.evidence: youtube/_redis.py:32 — redis.from_url(settings.REDIS_URL, decode_responses=True), no socket_timeout/socket_connect_timeout; billing/spend_guard.py:237, :365 (creator_block_status, reached from require_budget, a Depends on every LLM route); spend_guard.py:373-375 (except Exception -> fail open); limiter.py:18-49 (Issue 312 fixed exactly this for the OTHER Redis client); tests/test_rate_limiting.py:278 pins the timeout on the slowapi client only; docker-compose.prod.yml:14 (uvicorn --workers 2)
findings.failure_scenario: Redis is reachable but slow (BGSAVE fork, AOF rewrite, or the box's CPU saturated by two ffmpeg encodes). require_budget awaits r.ttl(cooldown_key) with no deadline and never returns. Both uvicorn workers saturate; each hung request also holds a checked-out DB session. The 'fail open on Redis error' arm is never reached because nothing raises — a hang is not an exception. The API goes unresponsive with no error, no log line, no 500, and a green /health.
findings.standard: Every Redis client in a request path carries a bounded socket_timeout and socket_connect_timeout; this project already established that as house standard in Issue 312 and applied it to one of its two clients. Also standard: a circuit breaker so a sustained outage stops hammering the dead dependency.
findings.verifier_note: Downgrade high → medium, and restate the mechanism. Accurate version: 'youtube/_redis.py:33 creates the shared async Redis singleton with no socket_timeout/socket_connect_timeout, making it the only one of the app''s four Redis clients without bounded timeouts (cf. limiter.py:83-86, main.py:100-101, routers/thumbnails.py:57). It is reached by billing/spend_guard.py:365 (creator_block_status, via the require_budget dependency on ~11 LLM/render routes), youtube/oauth.py''s token-refresh lock, and youtube/quota.py. Against a wedged-but-connected Redis, `await r.ttl(...)` (spend_guard.py:366) has no deadline, so the documented fail-open arm at :373-375 is never reached — a hang is not an exception. Because the client is asyncio, this does NOT block the event loop or saturate the uvicorn workers; the concrete cost is unbounded request lifetime holding a checked-out AsyncSession from Depends(get_current_creator), against a 20-connection pool per process (db.py). The common Redis-down case (co-located compose service → ECONNREFUSED/RST) raises immediately and fails open correctly, so the exposure is limited to the wedged-but-connected window. Fix is a one-liner: pass socket_timeout/socket_connect_timeout to redis.from_url, matching the values already used by the other three clients, plus a test that asserts the pool kwargs (mirroring tests/test_rate_limiting.py:278). Drop the circuit-breaker recommendation as out of scope for a ≤100-user single-VM beta.'

findings.evidence: models.py:279-318 (creator_api_keys), models.py:590-620 (creator_identity) — both FK creators.id ON DELETE CASCADE, neither in any CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation nor in migration 0010/0038/0040/0044/0045 table loops. Contrast models.py:1671-1673, :1723 and COMPLIANCE.md:108 which each carry an explicit 'no RLS, because' docstring. tests/test_rls_isolation_integration.py:265-284 is a hardcoded 17-name tuple; :579-586 a hardcoded 6-name tuple; zero repo-wide hits for pg_policies / relrowsecurity in tests/. Prior recurrences: OFF_COURSE_BUGS.md:46 and :25.
findings.failure_scenario: Any future handler that reads CreatorIdentity by primary key rather than by creator_id (the pattern routers/_owned.py exists to prevent, and which dna/identity.py:98 already uses for the supersede UPDATE ... WHERE CreatorIdentity.id == current.id) returns another creator's identity profile — mission, audience_summary, style_sample, hard_nos, all creator-authored free text that is injected into LLM prompts.
